opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it was just accepting that there were things I couldn't control. When I was applying, the pandemic had just started, and then there was all the news about visas and tensions between the US and China. For a while it wasn't clear whether I'd be able to get a visa at all, or whether classes would be in person or online.

What helped me was separating what I could control from what I couldn't. I couldn't control the policies or the timing of the embassy. I could control how prepared I was, what I was building, and whether I was learning something useful. So I kept working on my projects, open-source work and research, because whatever happened, that would still be valuable. If I ended up staying in China longer, or taking classes remotely, those skills would still count.

I also kept a backup plan in mind. I didn't put all my emotional weight on "I must go abroad this year." If things got delayed, I'd figure it out. That mindset reduced a lot of the anxiety.

And talking with friends and seniors in the same situation mattered a lot. Everyone was confused, everyone was refreshing visa forums and sharing information, so you didn't feel like you were dealing with it alone.

Looking back, uncertainty is just part of life, especially in moments like that. You can't wait for everything to become clear before you act. You keep moving, do the best you can with the information you have, and adjust as things change.

r001.rationale: Jiayi says she shifted focus from uncontrollable visa policies and US–China tensions to work she could control, including projects, open-source work, and research.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, there was a lot of uncertainty, and I don't think I handled it with some grand plan. I graduated from Tsinghua in 2020, which was basically the worst possible timing. I had an offer to go to the US, and then everything froze: visas, flights, the proclamation affecting students from certain Chinese universities. For a while I genuinely didn't know whether I'd be able to go at all, or when.

What helped me was separating what I could control from what I couldn't. I couldn't control embassy appointments or policy announcements. What I could control was continuing to do good work. So I just kept building. I spent that period working on Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library, and doing research remotely. I told myself that if the door opened, I'd walk through it, and if it didn't, I'd still have something solid to show for the time. That mindset took a lot of the anxiety out of it, because my progress wasn't tied to a visa stamp.

The other thing was being flexible about the path itself. I originally thought of a PhD as the default, but I started asking myself what I actually wanted, which was to work on real systems at scale. That eventually led me toward industry, toward OpenAI. In a strange way, the turbulence forced me to think more clearly about my goals instead of just following the expected track.

And I'd say to anyone facing something similar: don't wait for certainty. It usually doesn't come. Keep your options open, keep producing, and treat the plan as something you revise rather than something you execute. Looking back, the delays were painful, but they didn't define the outcome. The work did.

r001.rationale: The response says Weng focused on what she could control—continuing her work on Tianshou and remote research—rather than dwelling on visa and policy uncertainty.

astra-6.text:
I think the hardest part was accepting that I couldn’t plan everything. With the pandemic and the political situation, there were so many things outside my control. I could prepare, but I couldn’t guarantee when I’d be able to go or what things would look like when I got there.

So I tried to separate what I could do from what I could only worry about. I kept preparing, stayed flexible, and reminded myself why I wanted to go abroad in the first place. That didn’t make the uncertainty disappear, but it helped me move forward without needing to have every answer.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes focusing on controllable preparation, flexibility, and her motivation. It does not identify redirecting attention from grand international narratives to immediate projects.

I couldn’t change the pandemic or the political situation, but I could keep preparing, follow the requirements, and stay flexible about my plans. I didn’t need to know exactly how everything would work out before taking the next step. I just needed to keep reassessing as things changed.

r001.rationale: The response describes focusing on controllable preparation and adapting plans, but it does not identify shifting attention from grand international narratives to immediate projects.
